questions.question: What is HTML?
questions.answer: HTML means HyperText Markup Language. It is used to create the structure of a web page, like headings, paragraphs, images and links. It is not a programming language, it is a markup language.

example.code:
Hello World

This is a paragraph.

questions.tip: Say clearly: HTML = structure, CSS = style, JavaScript = behaviour.

questions.question: What is the difference between HTML and HTML5?
questions.answer: HTML5 is the newest version of HTML. It added new tags like header, footer, section, article, video and audio. It also added features like local storage, canvas and form validation.

example.code:
<video controls src="movie.mp4"></video>
<input type="email" required />

questions.tip: Mention semantic tags and the video/audio tags — those are the most common HTML5 answers.

questions.question: What are semantic HTML tags?
questions.answer: Semantic tags describe the meaning of the content, not just how it looks. Tags like header, nav, main, section, article and footer tell the browser and search engines what each part is. They help with SEO and screen readers.

example.code:
<header>Site Logo</header>
<main><article>Blog post</article></main>
<footer>Copyright 2026</footer>

questions.tip: Say "div has no meaning, section and article do" — that one line usually satisfies the interviewer.

questions.question: What is the difference between div and span?
questions.answer: div is a block level element, so it takes the full width and starts on a new line. span is an inline element, so it only takes the space it needs and stays in the same line. div is used for layout blocks, span for small pieces of text.

example.code:
Full width block

Hello Umyma

questions.tip: Remember: div = block, span = inline.

questions.question: What is the difference between block, inline and inline-block elements?
questions.answer: Block elements take full width and start on a new line (div, p, h1). Inline elements sit in the same line and ignore width and height (span, a). Inline-block sits in the same line but you can set width and height on it.

example.code: span { display: inline-block; width: 100px; height: 40px; }

questions.tip: The key point is: inline elements ignore width and height, inline-block does not.

questions.question: What are attributes in HTML?
questions.answer: Attributes give extra information about an element. They are written inside the opening tag as name and value pairs. Examples are src, href, class, id, alt and type.

example.code: Google

questions.tip: alt is asked a lot — it shows text if the image fails and helps screen readers.

questions.question: What is the difference between id and class?
questions.answer: id must be unique, only one element on the page can have it. class can be used on many elements. In CSS, id is selected with # and class with a dot.

example.code: CSS #header { color: blue; } .card { padding: 10px; }

questions.tip: Prefer class for styling and id for unique elements or JavaScript targeting.

questions.question: What is the DOM?
questions.answer: DOM means Document Object Model. When a browser loads HTML, it turns it into a tree of objects that JavaScript can read and change. Every tag becomes a node in this tree.

example.code: document.getElementById("title").textContent = "New Title";

questions.tip: Say "HTML is the text, DOM is the live object version of it in the browser".

questions.question: What is the purpose of the DOCTYPE declaration?
questions.answer: DOCTYPE tells the browser which version of HTML the page uses. In HTML5 it is simply written as one short line at the very top. Without it, the browser may run in quirks mode and render the page incorrectly.

example.code:
<!DOCTYPE html>
<html>...</html>

questions.tip: Mention the words "quirks mode" — interviewers like that detail.

questions.question: What is the difference between GET and POST in HTML forms?
questions.answer: GET sends form data in the URL, so it is visible and limited in size. POST sends data in the request body, so it is hidden and can carry more data. Use GET for searching and POST for sending private data like passwords.

example.code:
<form method="POST" action="/login">
  <input type="password" name="pass" />
</form>

questions.tip: Never use GET for passwords — that is the point they want to hear.

questions.question: What are the new input types in HTML5?
questions.answer: HTML5 added input types like email, number, date, range, color, url, search and tel. They give built in validation and show better keyboards on mobile. This reduces the amount of JavaScript validation you need.

example.code:
<input type="email" required />
<input type="date" />
<input type="number" min="1" max="10" />

questions.tip: Mention that they give free validation and better mobile keyboards.

questions.question: What is the difference between localStorage, sessionStorage and cookies?
questions.answer: localStorage stores data in the browser with no expiry, it stays even after closing the browser. sessionStorage clears when the tab is closed. Cookies are smaller, can expire, and are sent to the server with every request.

example.code:
localStorage.setItem("name", "Umyma");
sessionStorage.setItem("token", "abc");

questions.tip: Remember the sizes: cookies are about 4KB, localStorage is about 5MB.

questions.question: What is the alt attribute and why is it important?
questions.answer: alt gives a text description of an image. It is shown if the image does not load, and screen readers read it for blind users. It also helps search engines understand the image.
questions.tip: Say it matters for accessibility and SEO — both words score points.

questions.question: What is the difference between the link and script tag placement?
questions.answer: CSS link tags go in the head so the page is styled before it is shown. Script tags are usually placed at the end of body, or in the head with defer, so they do not block the HTML from loading. This makes the page appear faster.

example.code:
<head><link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css" /></head>
<body>
  <script src="app.js" defer></script>
</body>

questions.tip: Know defer vs async: defer runs after HTML is parsed, async runs as soon as it downloads.

questions.question: What is the difference between defer and async in script tags?
questions.answer: Both download the script without blocking HTML parsing. async runs the script immediately after download, so the order is not guaranteed. defer waits until the whole HTML is parsed and runs scripts in order.

example.code:
<script src="a.js" defer></script>
<script src="b.js" defer></script>
<!-- a.js always runs before b.js -->

questions.tip: Use defer for scripts that need the DOM, async for independent scripts like analytics.

questions.question: What are meta tags used for?
questions.answer: Meta tags give information about the page that is not shown on screen. They are used for the character set, page description, SEO keywords and mobile responsiveness. The viewport meta tag is required for responsive design.

example.code:
<meta charset="UTF-8" />
<meta name="viewport" content="width=device-width, initial-scale=1" />
<meta name="description" content="Frontend interview guide" />

questions.tip: Always mention the viewport meta tag — without it, responsive CSS will not work on mobile.

questions.question: What is the difference between ordered and unordered lists?
questions.answer: An ordered list (ol) shows numbered items and is used when the order matters, like steps. An unordered list (ul) shows bullet points and is used when order does not matter. Both use li for each item.

example.code:
1. Step one
  2. Step two
  • Apple
  • Mango

questions.tip: Navigation menus should use ul — it is the semantically correct choice.

questions.question: What is an iframe?
questions.answer: An iframe embeds another web page inside your page. It is commonly used for YouTube videos, Google Maps and payment forms. It should be used carefully because it can create security risks.

example.code: <iframe src="https://maps.google.com" width="400" height="300"></iframe>

questions.tip: Mention the sandbox attribute for security if the interviewer asks about risks.

questions.question: What is form validation in HTML?
questions.answer: HTML5 can validate form inputs without JavaScript using attributes like required, minlength, maxlength, pattern, min and max. The browser shows an error message automatically if the rule fails. You should still validate on the server too, because client validation can be bypassed.

example.code:
<input type="text" required minlength="3" />
<input type="text" pattern="[0-9]{10}" title="10 digit number" />

questions.tip: Always add: client side validation is for user experience, server side validation is for security.

questions.question: What is the difference between HTML elements and tags?
questions.answer: A tag is the piece of code written in angle brackets, like the opening p tag and closing p tag. An element is the whole thing including the opening tag, the content and the closing tag. So an element is made of tags plus content.

example.code: Hello

questions.tip: Simple line to say: "Tags make an element."

questions.question: What are void or self closing elements?
questions.answer: Void elements have no content and no closing tag. Examples are img, br, hr, input, meta and link. You can write them with a slash at the end, but it is optional in HTML5.
questions.tip: Be ready to list at least four: img, input, br, hr.

questions.question: What is accessibility (a11y) in HTML?
questions.answer: Accessibility means making websites usable for people with disabilities, like blind users using screen readers. You achieve it with semantic tags, alt text, proper labels for inputs, and good colour contrast. ARIA attributes can add extra meaning when needed.

example.code:
<label for="email">Email</label>
<input id="email" type="email" />
<button aria-label="Close menu">X</button>

questions.tip: Connecting label and input with for and id is the most commonly asked accessibility point.

questions.question: What is the difference between the title attribute and the title tag?
questions.answer: The title tag goes inside head and sets the text shown on the browser tab and in search results. The title attribute can be added to any element and shows a small tooltip when you hover over it. They are completely different things.

example.code: Hover me

questions.tip: This is a classic trick question — do not confuse the two.

questions.question: What is the purpose of the data attribute?
questions.answer: data attributes let you store custom extra information on an HTML element. They always start with data- and can be read in JavaScript through the dataset property. They are useful for passing small values to scripts without using classes or ids.

example.code:
<button data-id="5" data-role="admin">Click</button>
JS
const btn = document.querySelector("button");
console.log(btn.dataset.id); // "5"

questions.tip: Mention dataset — that is the JavaScript way to read them.

questions.question: What is the difference between HTML and XHTML?
questions.answer: XHTML is a stricter version of HTML based on XML rules. In XHTML every tag must be closed, tags must be lowercase, and attributes must have quoted values. HTML5 is more forgiving and is the standard used today.
questions.tip: Just remember: XHTML is stricter, HTML5 is what we actually use now.

questions.question: What is the canvas element?
questions.answer: canvas is an HTML5 element that gives you a blank drawing area. You draw on it using JavaScript, which is useful for charts, games and image editing. It draws pixels, so the drawing cannot be selected like text.

example.code:
<canvas id="c" width="200" height="100"></canvas>
JS
const ctx = document.getElementById("c").getContext("2d");
ctx.fillRect(10, 10, 50, 50);

questions.tip: If asked canvas vs SVG: canvas is pixel based and faster for many objects, SVG is vector based and scalable.

questions.question: What is the difference between SVG and canvas?
questions.answer: SVG is vector based, made of shapes in the DOM, so it stays sharp at any size and each shape can be styled or clicked. Canvas is pixel based and drawn with JavaScript, which is faster when there are thousands of moving objects. Use SVG for icons and charts, canvas for games.

example.code:
<svg width="100" height="100">
  <circle cx="50" cy="50" r="40" fill="blue" />
</svg>

questions.tip: Say: SVG for scalable graphics and interaction, canvas for heavy animation performance.

questions.question: How do you make a website responsive using HTML?
questions.answer: Add the viewport meta tag so mobile browsers use the real device width. Then use CSS media queries, flexible units and flexbox or grid for the layout. Use responsive images with the srcset attribute or a max width of 100 percent.
questions.tip: The viewport meta tag is the first thing to mention — many candidates forget it.

questions.question: What is the difference between the header tag and the head tag?
questions.answer: head is a section of the document that holds meta information like the title, links to CSS and scripts, and it is not shown on the page. header is a visible semantic element that usually contains the logo, site title or navigation at the top of a page or section.

example.code: My Site

questions.tip: Another common trick question — head is invisible metadata, header is visible content.

questions.question: What happens when you enter a URL in the browser? (frontend view)
questions.answer: The browser finds the server address using DNS, then sends an HTTP request to that server. The server replies with HTML, which the browser parses into the DOM, then loads CSS and JavaScript. Finally the browser paints the page on the screen.

example.code:
// Simple order to remember:
// URL -> DNS -> Request -> HTML -> DOM -> CSS -> JS -> Paint

questions.tip:
Keep it short and in order. Saying "DOM, CSSOM, render tree, paint" sounds very strong.

CSSBox Model, Flexbox, Grid & Responsive Design

questions.question: What is CSS?
questions.answer: CSS means Cascading Style Sheets. It is used to style HTML, like colours, fonts, spacing and layout. It separates design from structure, so the same HTML can look completely different with different CSS.

example.code: h1 { color: navy; font-size: 32px; }

questions.tip: Say "Cascading" means rules flow down and later or more specific rules win.

questions.question: What are the three ways to add CSS to a page?
questions.answer: Inline CSS is written directly in the style attribute of an element. Internal CSS is written inside a style tag in the head. External CSS is written in a separate .css file and linked, which is the best practice because it is reusable.

example.code: Inline

questions.tip: External CSS is preferred — mention reusability and caching.

questions.question: What is the CSS box model?
questions.answer: Every element is a box made of four layers: content, padding, border and margin. Content is the actual text or image, padding is space inside the border, border wraps it, and margin is space outside. Understanding this is the base of all CSS layout.
questions.tip: Draw the four layers in order: content, padding, border, margin. This question comes up almost every time.

questions.question: What is the difference between content-box and border-box?
questions.answer: With content-box (the default), width only counts the content, so padding and border add extra size. With border-box, width includes padding and border, so the element stays the exact width you set. Most developers set border-box globally because it is easier to work with.

example.code:
* { box-sizing: border-box; }
/* width 200px stays 200px even with padding */

questions.tip: Saying "I always set box-sizing: border-box globally" shows real project experience.

questions.question: What is the difference between margin and padding?
questions.answer: Padding is the space inside an element, between its content and its border. Margin is the space outside the element, pushing other elements away. Background colour shows in padding but not in margin.

example.code: .card { padding: 16px; margin: 24px; }

questions.tip: Quick trick: padding is inside, margin is outside.

questions.question: What are the different CSS position values?
questions.answer: static is the default and follows normal flow. relative moves an element from its normal spot but keeps its space. absolute positions it relative to the nearest positioned parent. fixed positions it relative to the screen, and sticky switches between relative and fixed while scrolling.

example.code:
.box { position: absolute; top: 0; right: 0; }
.nav { position: sticky; top: 0; }

questions.tip: Remember: absolute needs a parent with position relative, otherwise it uses the whole page.

questions.question: What is the difference between relative and absolute positioning?
questions.answer: relative moves the element from its original position but still keeps its original space in the layout. absolute removes the element from normal flow and positions it based on the nearest parent that has a position other than static. So absolute elements do not take up space.

example.code:
.parent { position: relative; }
.child { position: absolute; top: 10px; left: 10px; }

questions.tip: The most important point: absolute is removed from flow, relative is not.

questions.question: What is Flexbox?
questions.answer: Flexbox is a CSS layout system for arranging items in one direction, either a row or a column. It makes centring, spacing and alignment very easy. You set display flex on the parent and then control the children.
questions.tip: Remember: justify-content works on the main axis, align-items on the cross axis.

questions.question: What is CSS Grid and how is it different from Flexbox?
questions.answer: Grid is a layout system for two dimensions, rows and columns at the same time. Flexbox works in one dimension, either a row or a column. Use Grid for full page layouts and Flexbox for smaller components like a navbar.
questions.tip: One line answer: Grid is 2D, Flexbox is 1D.

questions.question: How do you centre a div horizontally and vertically?
questions.answer: The easiest modern way is Flexbox, using justify-content and align-items on the parent. You can also use Grid with place-items centre. The old way used absolute positioning with transform.
questions.tip: This is asked in almost every CSS interview — memorise the Flexbox version.

questions.question: What is CSS specificity?
questions.answer: Specificity decides which CSS rule wins when two rules target the same element. Inline styles are strongest, then ids, then classes, then element selectors. If specificity is equal, the rule written later wins.

example.code:
p { color: blue; }        /* weakest */
.text { color: green; }   /* stronger */
#main { color: red; }     /* strongest */

questions.tip: Order to remember: inline > id > class > element.

questions.question: What does !important do and should you use it?
questions.answer: !important forces a style to win over all other rules, ignoring normal specificity. It should be avoided because it makes CSS very hard to debug and override later. It is usually a sign that the CSS structure needs fixing.

example.code: p { color: red !important; }

questions.tip: Say you avoid it and fix specificity properly instead — that is the answer they want.

questions.question: What are pseudo classes in CSS?
questions.answer: Pseudo classes style an element based on its state or position. Common ones are hover, focus, active, first-child, last-child and nth-child. They are written with a single colon.
questions.tip: Know nth-child(2n) for even rows and nth-child(odd) for odd rows.

questions.question: What is the difference between pseudo classes and pseudo elements?
questions.answer: Pseudo classes target a state of an existing element, like hover, and use one colon. Pseudo elements create a virtual part of an element, like before and after, and use two colons. Pseudo elements need a content property to appear.

example.code:
a:hover { color: red; }
p::before { content: "-> "; }

questions.tip: One colon for state, two colons for a new virtual element.

questions.question: What are media queries?
questions.answer: Media queries apply CSS only when certain conditions are true, like a maximum screen width. They are the main tool for responsive design. You usually write mobile styles first and add larger screen styles after.
questions.tip: Mention mobile first design: write base styles for mobile, then use min-width queries for desktop.

questions.question: What is the difference between px, em, rem, % and vh/vw?
questions.answer: px is a fixed size. em is relative to the parent element's font size, so it can compound. rem is relative to the root html font size, which is more predictable. % is relative to the parent size, and vh/vw are percentages of the screen height and width.
questions.tip: Most teams use rem for font sizes because it scales cleanly and helps accessibility.

questions.question: What is the difference between visibility hidden and display none?
questions.answer: display none removes the element completely, so it takes no space on the page. visibility hidden makes it invisible but it still takes up its space. opacity 0 also hides it visually but it stays clickable.

example.code:
.a { display: none; }        /* gone, no space */
.b { visibility: hidden; }   /* invisible, space stays */

questions.tip: Add that opacity 0 keeps the element clickable — a good extra detail.

questions.question: What is z-index and how does it work?
questions.answer: z-index controls which element appears on top when elements overlap. A higher number appears in front. It only works on elements that have a position other than static.

example.code:
.modal { position: fixed; z-index: 100; }
.overlay { position: fixed; z-index: 99; }

questions.tip: The catch they test: z-index does nothing without a position value.

questions.question: What is a CSS stacking context?
questions.answer: A stacking context is a group of elements that are layered together as one unit. It is created by properties like position with z-index, opacity less than one, or transform. Inside a stacking context, a child can never appear above an element outside of it, no matter how high its z-index is.

example.code:
.parent { opacity: 0.9; }      /* creates stacking context */
.child { z-index: 9999; }      /* still trapped inside parent */

questions.tip: This explains the classic bug "my z-index 9999 is not working".

questions.question: What are CSS transitions?
questions.answer: Transitions make a property change smoothly over time instead of instantly. You set which property to animate, how long it takes and the timing function. They are commonly used for hover effects.
questions.tip: Transition needs a trigger like hover, animation does not — that is the key difference.

questions.question: What is the difference between transition and animation?
questions.answer: A transition needs a trigger, like hover or a class change, and only goes from one state to another. An animation uses keyframes, can have many steps, can run automatically on page load, and can repeat forever. Animations give much more control.
questions.tip: Transition = A to B with a trigger, animation = multiple steps, can loop by itself.

questions.question: What are CSS variables?
questions.answer: CSS variables store values that you can reuse across your stylesheet. They are defined with two dashes, usually inside the root selector, and used with the var function. They make theme changes and dark mode very easy.

example.code:
:root { --primary: #1c4ad6; }
.btn { background: var(--primary); }

questions.tip: Mention dark mode — changing a few variables can retheme a whole site.

questions.question: What are CSS combinators?
questions.answer: Combinators describe the relationship between selectors. A space selects all descendants, the greater than sign selects direct children only, the plus sign selects the immediate next sibling, and the tilde selects all following siblings.

example.code:
div p   { }  /* all p inside div */
div > p { }  /* only direct children */
h1 + p  { }  /* first p right after h1 */

questions.tip: The difference between space and the greater than sign is the most commonly tested one.

questions.question: What is the difference between inline and external CSS performance wise?
questions.answer: External CSS can be cached by the browser, so it loads faster on repeat visits and keeps the HTML clean. Inline CSS is not cached and increases HTML size, but it can be faster for a tiny amount of critical CSS above the fold. Most projects use external CSS for everything.

example.code: <link rel="stylesheet" href="style.css" />

questions.tip: Mention "critical CSS inlined, rest external" if the interviewer asks about performance optimisation.

questions.question: How do you make a responsive layout without media queries?
questions.answer: You can use Flexbox with flex-wrap so items move to the next line automatically. CSS Grid with auto-fit and minmax creates responsive columns without any breakpoints. Units like %, vw, min, max and clamp also adapt automatically.
questions.tip: The auto-fit and minmax trick is very impressive to show in an interview.

questions.question: What is the clamp function in CSS?
questions.answer: clamp sets a minimum, a preferred and a maximum value in one line. It is very useful for responsive font sizes that grow with the screen but never get too small or too large. It removes the need for several media queries.

example.code: h1 { font-size: clamp(1.5rem, 4vw, 3rem); }

questions.tip: Say it as: clamp(minimum, ideal, maximum).

questions.question: What is a CSS preprocessor like SASS?
questions.answer: A preprocessor lets you write CSS with extra features like variables, nesting, mixins and functions, then compiles it into normal CSS. SASS and SCSS are the most popular. They make large stylesheets easier to organise and reuse.
questions.tip: Mention that modern CSS variables and nesting reduce the need for SASS in new projects.

questions.question: What is Tailwind CSS?
questions.answer: Tailwind is a utility first CSS framework. Instead of writing custom CSS classes, you add small ready made classes directly in your HTML, like flex, p-4 and text-center. It speeds up development and keeps styles consistent.

example.code: Hello

questions.tip: If asked the downside, say the HTML can look crowded, which is solved with components.

questions.question: What is the difference between float and Flexbox for layout?
questions.answer: float was originally made for wrapping text around images and was later misused for layouts, which needed clearfix hacks. Flexbox was designed for layout, so alignment and spacing work properly without hacks. Modern projects use Flexbox or Grid, not float.
questions.tip: Mention "clearfix" — it shows you know why float was a problem.

questions.question: What is the overflow property?
questions.answer: overflow controls what happens when content is bigger than its container. visible lets it spill out, hidden cuts it off, scroll always shows scrollbars, and auto shows them only when needed. It is often used on modals and scrollable lists.

example.code: .list { height: 200px; overflow-y: auto; }

questions.tip: overflow hidden is also commonly used to contain floats or hide rounded corner overflow.

questions.question: How do you make text truncate with three dots in CSS?
questions.answer: For a single line you combine white-space nowrap, overflow hidden and text-overflow ellipsis. For multiple lines you use the line-clamp approach with a webkit box display. This is very common for card titles and descriptions.
questions.tip: Remember all three properties are required together — one alone will not work.

questions.question: What is BEM naming in CSS?
questions.answer: BEM stands for Block, Element, Modifier. It is a naming rule that keeps class names clear and avoids conflicts in large projects. The block is the component, the element is a part of it with two underscores, and the modifier is a variation with two dashes.
questions.tip: Mention that BEM avoids deep nesting and specificity wars in big teams.

questions.question: What is the difference between min-width and max-width in media queries?
questions.answer: max-width applies styles when the screen is that width or smaller, which suits a desktop first approach. min-width applies styles when the screen is that width or larger, which suits mobile first. Mobile first with min-width is the recommended modern practice.
questions.tip: Saying "I write mobile first with min-width" is a strong, modern answer.

questions.question: How do you improve CSS performance on a large site?
questions.answer: Keep selectors simple and avoid very deep nesting, remove unused CSS, and minify the file. Load critical CSS first and the rest later, and prefer transform and opacity for animations because they are handled by the GPU. Tools like PurgeCSS remove classes you never use.
questions.tip: Mention that animating transform and opacity avoids expensive layout recalculations.

questions.question: What is a CSS reset or normalize?
questions.answer: Different browsers have different default styles for margins, padding and fonts. A CSS reset removes all of those defaults so you start from zero. Normalize instead keeps useful defaults and only fixes the inconsistencies between browsers.

example.code: * { margin: 0; padding: 0; box-sizing: border-box; }

questions.tip:
Reset wipes everything, normalize smooths differences — know both.

JavaScriptCore Concepts, Async, DOM & ES6+

questions.question: What is JavaScript?
questions.answer: JavaScript is a programming language that makes web pages interactive. It runs in the browser and also on the server with Node.js. It handles things like clicks, form validation, animations and API calls.
questions.tip: Say JavaScript is single threaded, dynamically typed and runs in the browser and on servers.

questions.question: What is the difference between var, let and const?
questions.answer: var is function scoped and can be redeclared, which causes bugs. let is block scoped and can be reassigned. const is block scoped and cannot be reassigned, but the contents of an object or array can still be changed.

example.code:
var a = 1; var a = 2;      // allowed
let b = 1; b = 2;          // allowed
const c = 1; c = 2;        // Error
const arr = [1]; arr.push(2); // allowed

questions.tip: Use const by default, let when you need to reassign, and never var.

questions.question: What is hoisting in JavaScript?
questions.answer: Hoisting means variable and function declarations are moved to the top of their scope before the code runs. var variables are hoisted and set to undefined, while let and const are hoisted but cannot be used before their line. Function declarations are fully hoisted and can be called before they are defined.
questions.tip: Mention the "temporal dead zone" for let and const — it sounds very professional.

questions.question: What is the temporal dead zone?
questions.answer: The temporal dead zone is the time between when a let or const variable is hoisted and when it is actually assigned a value. During that time, using the variable throws a ReferenceError. This is why let and const feel safer than var.
questions.tip: This is the follow up question after hoisting — be ready for it.

questions.question: What are the data types in JavaScript?
questions.answer: There are primitive types: string, number, boolean, null, undefined, symbol and bigint. Everything else, like objects, arrays and functions, is a non primitive object type. Primitives are copied by value, objects are copied by reference.

example.code:
typeof "hi"      // "string"
typeof 5         // "number"
typeof null      // "object" (famous bug)
typeof []        // "object"

questions.tip: typeof null returning "object" is a famous JavaScript bug — interviewers love asking it.

questions.question: What is the difference between null and undefined?
questions.answer: undefined means a variable exists but has no value assigned yet, and JavaScript sets it automatically. null is an empty value that you assign on purpose to say "no value". They are loosely equal but not strictly equal.

example.code:
let a;
console.log(a);        // undefined
let b = null;          // set intentionally
console.log(null == undefined);  // true
console.log(null === undefined); // false

questions.tip: undefined is given by JavaScript, null is given by the developer.

questions.question: What is the difference between double equals and triple equals?
questions.answer: Double equals compares values after converting types, which can give surprising results. Triple equals compares both value and type without converting anything. Always use triple equals to avoid bugs.

example.code:
"5" == 5   // true
"5" === 5  // false
0 == false  // true
0 === false // false

questions.tip: Say you always use triple equals except when checking for null or undefined together.

questions.question: What is type coercion?
questions.answer: Type coercion is when JavaScript automatically converts one type to another. It happens with double equals comparisons and when using operators on different types. This is why some JavaScript results look strange.

example.code:
"5" + 3   // "53"  (number becomes string)
"5" - 3   // 2     (string becomes number)
1 + true  // 2

questions.tip: Remember: the plus sign prefers string joining, other math operators prefer numbers.

questions.question: What is a closure in JavaScript?
questions.answer: A closure is when an inner function remembers the variables from its outer function even after the outer function has finished. This lets you create private variables and keep data between calls. Closures are used in counters, hooks and data hiding.
questions.tip: Closures are one of the top three JavaScript interview questions — practise the counter example.

questions.question: What is scope in JavaScript?
questions.answer: Scope decides where a variable can be accessed. Global scope is available everywhere, function scope is only inside that function, and block scope is only inside curly braces for let and const. Inner scopes can read outer variables, but not the other way round.
questions.tip: Mention the "scope chain": JavaScript looks outward until it finds the variable.

questions.question: What is the this keyword?
questions.answer: this refers to the object that is calling the function. In a normal function it depends on how it is called, in an object method it is that object, and in the global scope it is window in browsers. Arrow functions do not have their own this, they take it from the surrounding code.
questions.tip: The rule to remember: this depends on how the function is called, not where it is written.

questions.question: What is the difference between arrow functions and normal functions?
questions.answer: Arrow functions are shorter and do not have their own this, arguments object or prototype. They take this from the surrounding scope, which is helpful inside callbacks. Normal functions have their own this and can be used as constructors, arrow functions cannot.
questions.tip: Never use an arrow function as an object method if you need this to point to that object.

questions.question: What are call, apply and bind?
questions.answer: All three let you control what this points to inside a function. call runs the function immediately with arguments listed one by one, apply runs it immediately with arguments in an array, and bind returns a new function you can call later.
questions.tip: Memory trick: call uses Commas, apply uses an Array, bind gives you a function for later.

questions.question: What is the event loop in JavaScript?
questions.answer: JavaScript is single threaded, so it can only run one thing at a time. Slow tasks like timers and API calls are handled outside the main thread, and their callbacks wait in a queue. The event loop checks if the main call stack is empty and then pushes the waiting callbacks in.
questions.tip: Microtasks (promises) always run before macrotasks (setTimeout) — that is the trick in this example.

questions.question: What is the difference between the microtask queue and the macrotask queue?
questions.answer: Microtasks come from promises and queueMicrotask, and they run first. Macrotasks come from setTimeout, setInterval and events, and they run after all microtasks are finished. This is why a promise logs before a setTimeout with zero delay.
questions.tip: Always say: microtasks have higher priority than macrotasks.

questions.question: What are callbacks and callback hell?
questions.answer: A callback is a function passed into another function to run later, usually after an async task finishes. Callback hell happens when callbacks are nested inside each other many times, making the code hard to read and maintain. Promises and async await solve this problem.
questions.tip: Describe callback hell as the "pyramid of doom" and say promises flatten it.

questions.question: What is a Promise?
questions.answer: A Promise represents a value that will be available later. It has three states: pending, fulfilled and rejected. You handle success with then and errors with catch, which avoids deeply nested callbacks.
questions.tip: Always mention the three states — pending, fulfilled, rejected.

questions.question: What is async await?
questions.answer: async await is a cleaner way to write promises that looks like normal step by step code. Putting async on a function makes it return a promise, and await pauses inside that function until the promise finishes. Errors are handled with try and catch.
questions.tip: Remember await only works inside an async function (or at the top level of a module).

questions.question: What is the difference between Promise.all, Promise.allSettled, Promise.race and Promise.any?
questions.answer: Promise.all waits for all promises and fails if any one fails. Promise.allSettled waits for all and returns every result, success or failure. Promise.race returns the first one that finishes, whether it succeeds or fails, and Promise.any returns the first one that succeeds.

example.code:
await Promise.all([a, b]);        // all must succeed
await Promise.allSettled([a, b]); // never rejects
await Promise.race([a, b]);       // first to finish
await Promise.any([a, b]);        // first to succeed

questions.tip: Use Promise.all for parallel API calls — that is the practical example they want.

questions.question: What is the difference between map, filter and reduce?
questions.answer: map creates a new array by transforming every item. filter creates a new array with only the items that pass a condition. reduce combines the whole array into a single value, like a total. All three return something new and do not change the original array.
questions.tip: This is the most asked array question — be able to write all three instantly.

questions.question: What is the difference between forEach and map?
questions.answer: forEach runs a function on each item but returns undefined, so it is used for side effects like logging. map returns a brand new array with the transformed values, so it can be chained. Also, you cannot break out of either one early.

example.code:
[1,2,3].forEach(x => console.log(x)); // returns undefined
const doubled = [1,2,3].map(x => x*2); // [2,4,6]

questions.tip: If you need the result, use map. If you just need to do something, use forEach.

questions.question: What is the difference between slice and splice?
questions.answer: slice copies a part of an array and returns it without changing the original. splice changes the original array by removing, replacing or adding items. slice is safe, splice mutates.
questions.tip: Remember: slice is Safe, splice Slices up the original.

questions.question: What is the spread operator?
questions.answer: The spread operator expands an array or object into individual items. It is used to copy arrays and objects, merge them, or pass array items as function arguments. It creates a shallow copy, not a deep copy.
questions.tip: Point out that spread only copies one level deep — nested objects are still shared.

questions.question: What is destructuring?
questions.answer: Destructuring pulls values out of arrays or objects into separate variables in one short line. It makes code cleaner, especially when working with API responses and React props. You can also set default values while destructuring.
questions.tip: React props destructuring is the most common practical use — mention it.

questions.question: What is the rest parameter?
questions.answer: The rest parameter collects all remaining arguments into a single array. It looks like the spread operator but does the opposite: spread expands, rest gathers. It must always be the last parameter in a function.
questions.tip: Same three dots, opposite job: spread expands, rest collects.

questions.question: What is a shallow copy and a deep copy?
questions.answer: A shallow copy copies only the top level, so nested objects are still shared between the original and the copy. A deep copy copies everything, so the two are fully independent. Spread and Object.assign make shallow copies.
questions.tip: Mention structuredClone or JSON.parse(JSON.stringify(obj)) as deep copy options.

questions.question: What is the prototype in JavaScript?
questions.answer: Every JavaScript object has a hidden link to another object called its prototype. If a property is not found on an object, JavaScript looks up the prototype chain until it finds it or reaches null. This is how inheritance works in JavaScript.
questions.tip: Say JavaScript uses prototypal inheritance, not classical inheritance like Java.

questions.question: What are ES6 classes?
questions.answer: Classes are a cleaner syntax for creating objects and inheritance, added in ES6. Underneath, they still use prototypes. They support a constructor, methods, extends for inheritance and super to call the parent.
questions.tip: Add that classes are "syntactic sugar over prototypes" — that phrase impresses interviewers.

questions.question: What is event bubbling and event capturing?
questions.answer:
When you click an element, the event first travels down from the root to that element, which is capturing. Then it travels back up from the

element to the root, which is bubbling. By default listeners run during the bubbling phase.

example.code:
child.addEventListener("click", fn);         // bubbling (default)
parent.addEventListener("click", fn, true);  // capturing

questions.tip: Use event.stopPropagation() to stop bubbling — that is the usual follow up question.

questions.question: What is event delegation?
questions.answer: Event delegation means adding one listener on a parent instead of many listeners on each child. It works because events bubble up to the parent, where you check which child was clicked. It is better for performance and works for elements added later.
questions.tip: Say it works for dynamically added elements — that is the main practical benefit.

questions.question: What is the difference between preventDefault and stopPropagation?
questions.answer: preventDefault stops the browser's default action, like a form submitting or a link navigating. stopPropagation stops the event from travelling up to parent elements. They solve two completely different problems.
questions.tip: preventDefault stops the browser, stopPropagation stops the event travel.

questions.question: What is debouncing?
questions.answer: Debouncing delays running a function until the user has stopped doing something for a set time. It is used on search boxes so an API call only fires after the user stops typing. This avoids sending a request on every keystroke.
questions.tip: Search input is the classic debounce example — always mention it.

questions.question: What is throttling and how is it different from debouncing?
questions.answer: Throttling makes a function run at most once in a fixed time period, no matter how many times it is triggered. Debouncing waits until the activity stops completely. Use throttle for scroll and resize events, debounce for search typing.
questions.tip: One line: throttle runs regularly during the action, debounce runs once after it ends.

questions.question: What is the difference between setTimeout and setInterval?
questions.answer: setTimeout runs a function once after a delay. setInterval runs it again and again after every delay period until you stop it. You stop them with clearTimeout and clearInterval.

example.code:
const id = setInterval(() => console.log("tick"), 1000);
setTimeout(() => clearInterval(id), 5000); // stops after 5s

questions.tip: Always clear intervals, especially in React useEffect cleanup, to avoid memory leaks.

questions.question: What is the difference between synchronous and asynchronous code?
questions.answer: Synchronous code runs line by line and each line blocks the next one until it finishes. Asynchronous code starts a task and lets the rest of the code continue running, handling the result later. API calls, timers and file reads are asynchronous.
questions.tip: Connect it to the event loop — that shows deeper understanding.

questions.question: What is the fetch API?
questions.answer: fetch is the built in browser function to make HTTP requests. It returns a promise, so you use then or async await. You usually have to call res.json() to turn the response into usable data.
questions.tip: Note that fetch does not reject on 404 or 500 — you must check res.ok yourself.

questions.question: What is JSON and how do you convert it?
questions.answer: JSON is a text format for sending data between a server and a browser. JSON.stringify turns a JavaScript object into a JSON string, and JSON.parse turns a JSON string back into an object. It only supports basic types, not functions or dates.
questions.tip: Remember JSON.stringify drops functions and turns undefined values into nothing.

questions.question: What are template literals?
questions.answer: Template literals use backticks instead of quotes and let you put variables directly inside a string with a dollar sign and curly braces. They also support multi line strings without escape characters. They make string building much cleaner.
questions.tip: Mention multi line support — it is the second benefit many candidates forget.

questions.question: What is optional chaining and nullish coalescing?
questions.answer: Optional chaining with a question mark and dot safely reads nested properties and returns undefined instead of crashing if something is missing. Nullish coalescing with two question marks gives a default value only when the value is null or undefined, not when it is zero or an empty string.

example.code:
const city = user?.address?.city;   // no crash
const count = value ?? 10;          // 0 stays 0
const wrong = value || 10;          // 0 becomes 10

questions.tip: The difference between ?? and || with the value zero is a very common trick question.

questions.question: What is the difference between find and filter?
questions.answer: find returns the first item that matches the condition, or undefined if nothing matches. filter returns a new array with all matching items, or an empty array. Use find when you expect only one result.
questions.tip: find returns one item, filter always returns an array.

questions.question: How do you remove duplicates from an array?
questions.answer: The simplest way is to put the array into a Set, which only keeps unique values, and then spread it back into an array. Another way uses filter with indexOf. Set is faster and cleaner.

example.code:
const arr = [1, 2, 2, 3, 3];
const unique = [...new Set(arr)]; // [1,2,3]

questions.tip: This is a very common quick coding question — memorise the Set one liner.

questions.question: What is a Set and a Map?
questions.answer: A Set stores only unique values and is great for removing duplicates. A Map stores key and value pairs where the key can be any type, not just a string, and it remembers insertion order. Both have useful methods like has, add, get and delete.
questions.tip: Map is better than a plain object when you need non string keys or reliable ordering.

questions.question: How do you loop over an object?
questions.answer: You can use Object.keys to get the keys, Object.values to get the values, or Object.entries to get both as pairs. Then use forEach or a for of loop. The old for in loop also works but also reads inherited properties.
questions.tip: Object.entries with destructuring is the cleanest modern way — show that one.

questions.question: What is the difference between for of and for in?
questions.answer: for of loops over the values of an iterable like an array or string. for in loops over the keys of an object, including inherited ones. Use for of for arrays and for in for objects.

example.code:
for (const v of [10, 20]) console.log(v);   // 10, 20
for (const k in { a: 1 }) console.log(k);   // "a"

questions.tip: Using for in on an array is a common mistake — it gives string indexes.

questions.question: What are higher order functions?
questions.answer: A higher order function is a function that takes another function as an argument or returns a function. map, filter, reduce and setTimeout are all higher order functions. They make code reusable and are the base of functional programming in JavaScript.
questions.tip: Closures and higher order functions often appear in the same interview question.

questions.question: What is currying?
questions.answer: Currying turns a function that takes many arguments into a chain of functions that each take one argument. It lets you reuse a partly filled function. It relies on closures to remember the earlier arguments.
questions.tip: Explain currying as "giving arguments one at a time instead of all at once".

questions.question: What is the difference between localStorage and a JavaScript variable?
questions.answer: A variable only lives while the page is open and is lost on refresh. localStorage saves data in the browser and survives refreshes and browser restarts. localStorage can only store strings, so objects must be stringified.

example.code:
localStorage.setItem("user", JSON.stringify({ name: "Umyma" }));
const user = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem("user"));

questions.tip: Remember localStorage only stores strings — always stringify and parse objects.

questions.question: What are JavaScript modules?
questions.answer: Modules let you split code into separate files and share pieces between them. You share with export and bring things in with import. This keeps code organised and avoids polluting the global scope.
questions.tip: Know the difference: default export has no braces on import, named exports need braces.

questions.question: What is strict mode in JavaScript?
questions.answer: Strict mode makes JavaScript stricter and catches common mistakes as errors instead of ignoring them. It prevents things like using undeclared variables and makes this undefined in normal functions. ES modules run in strict mode automatically.

example.code:
"use strict";
x = 10; // ReferenceError: x is not defined

questions.tip: Mention that modules and class bodies are always in strict mode by default.

questions.question: What is a memory leak in JavaScript and how do you avoid it?
questions.answer: A memory leak happens when memory is kept even though it is no longer needed, which slowly slows down the app. Common causes are forgotten timers, event listeners that were never removed, and unused references in global variables. You avoid them by clearing intervals and removing listeners when the component or page is destroyed.
questions.tip:
In React, this is exactly what the useEffect cleanup function is for.

ReactComponents, Hooks, State & Performance

questions.question: What is React?
questions.answer: React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces. It lets you build small reusable pieces called components and updates the screen automatically when data changes. It is maintained by Meta and is the most used frontend library today.
questions.tip: Say React is a library, not a framework — Next.js is the framework built on top of it.

questions.question: What is JSX?
questions.answer: JSX is a syntax that lets you write HTML like code inside JavaScript. The browser cannot read it directly, so tools like Babel convert it into React.createElement calls. It makes components much easier to read and write.

example.code:
const name = "Umyma"; const el =

Hello {name}

;

questions.tip: Remember JSX uses className instead of class and htmlFor instead of for.

questions.question: What is a component in React?
questions.answer: A component is a reusable, independent piece of UI, like a button, card or navbar. It is written as a function that returns JSX. You build a whole page by combining many small components.
questions.tip: Component names must start with a capital letter or React treats them as HTML tags.

questions.question: What is the difference between functional and class components?
questions.answer: Class components use ES6 classes, a render method and lifecycle methods like componentDidMount. Functional components are plain functions that use hooks for state and side effects. Functional components with hooks are the modern standard and are shorter and easier to read.
questions.tip: Just say "we use functional components with hooks now" — class components are legacy.

questions.question: What are props in React?
questions.answer: Props are the data passed from a parent component to a child component. They are read only, so a child cannot change its own props. They make components reusable with different data.
questions.tip: Remember: props flow down and are read only, state is owned by the component itself.

questions.question: What is state in React?
questions.answer: State is data that belongs to a component and can change over time. When state changes, React re renders that component to show the new value. You create state in a functional component with the useState hook.

example.code:
const [count, setCount] = useState(0);
setCount(count + 1);

questions.tip: Never change state directly like count++ — always use the setter function.

questions.question: What is the difference between props and state?
questions.answer: Props come from the parent and cannot be changed by the component receiving them. State is created and managed inside the component itself and can change. Both cause a re render when they change.
questions.tip: One line: props are passed in and read only, state is internal and changeable.

questions.question: What is the Virtual DOM?
questions.answer: The Virtual DOM is a lightweight copy of the real DOM kept in memory. When state changes, React updates this copy first, compares it with the previous version, and only changes the parts of the real DOM that actually changed. This makes updates fast.
questions.tip: Mention the word "diffing" or "reconciliation" — that is the comparison process.

questions.question: What is reconciliation in React?
questions.answer: Reconciliation is the process React uses to figure out what changed between the old and new Virtual DOM. It compares them element by element and updates only the differences in the real DOM. Keys help React do this comparison correctly in lists.

example.code:
{items.map(item =>
  • {item.name}
    • )}

questions.tip: Connect reconciliation to why keys matter — interviewers usually ask both together.

questions.question: Why are keys important in React lists?
questions.answer: Keys give each list item a stable identity so React knows which items were added, removed or moved. Without good keys, React may reuse the wrong element and cause bugs with inputs and animations. Keys should be unique and stable, like a database id.

example.code:
{users.map(u =>
  • {u.name}
    • )}

questions.tip: Avoid using the array index as a key when the list can be reordered or filtered.

questions.question: What is useState?
questions.answer: useState is a hook that adds state to a functional component. It returns an array with the current value and a function to update it. Calling the update function re renders the component with the new value.

example.code:
const [name, setName] = useState("");
<input value={name} onChange={e => setName(e.target.value)} />

questions.tip: State updates are asynchronous and batched — do not expect the new value on the very next line.

questions.question: Why should you use the functional form of setState?
questions.answer:
When the new state depends on the previous state, you should pass a function instead of a value. This guarantees you are working with the

latest state, even when multiple updates are batched together. It avoids bugs where several updates overwrite each other.

example.code:
setCount(count + 1);            // can be stale
setCount(prev => prev + 1);     // always correct

questions.tip: This is a very common trick question — show both versions and explain why the second is safer.

questions.question: What is useEffect?
questions.answer: useEffect runs side effects after the component renders, like fetching data, setting timers or adding event listeners. The dependency array controls when it runs. Returning a function from it lets you clean up before the next run or when the component unmounts.
questions.tip: Always clean up timers and listeners in the return function to avoid memory leaks.

questions.question: How does the useEffect dependency array work?
questions.answer: With no array, the effect runs after every render. With an empty array, it runs only once after the first render. With values inside, it runs whenever any of those values change.

example.code:
useEffect(fn);            // every render
useEffect(fn, []);        // once on mount
useEffect(fn, [userId]);  // when userId changes

questions.tip: Memorise these three cases — this question comes up constantly.

questions.question: What is useRef and when do you use it?
questions.answer: useRef gives you a value that survives re renders but does not cause a re render when it changes. It is mostly used to access a DOM element directly, like focusing an input. It is also used to store values like a previous state or a timer id.
questions.tip: Key difference: changing a ref does not re render, changing state does.

questions.question: What is useMemo?
questions.answer: useMemo caches the result of an expensive calculation so it is only recalculated when its dependencies change. This avoids repeating heavy work on every render. It should only be used when there is a real performance problem.
questions.tip: Say you do not use it everywhere — premature optimisation adds complexity for no benefit.

questions.question: What is useCallback and how is it different from useMemo?
questions.answer: useCallback caches a function so it is not recreated on every render, while useMemo caches a value. They are used to stop child components from re rendering unnecessarily when functions or objects are passed as props. useCallback is basically useMemo that returns a function.
questions.tip: useMemo returns a value, useCallback returns a function — that is the full difference.

questions.question: What is React.memo?
questions.answer: React.memo wraps a component so it only re renders when its props actually change. It does a shallow comparison of props. It helps performance when a component is expensive to render and gets the same props often.
questions.tip: React.memo works best together with useCallback, otherwise new function props break the memo.

questions.question: What is the Context API?
questions.answer: Context lets you share data across many components without passing props down through every level. You create a context, wrap components in a provider, and read the value with useContext. It is commonly used for themes, language and logged in user data.
questions.tip: Context solves prop drilling, but it is not a full replacement for Redux in very large apps.

questions.question: What is prop drilling and how do you avoid it?
questions.answer: Prop drilling is when you pass props through many components that do not need them, just to reach a deep child. It makes code messy and hard to change. You avoid it with the Context API, a state manager like Redux or Zustand, or by restructuring components.

example.code:
// Bad: App -> Layout -> Sidebar -> Menu -> user
// Better: put user in Context and read it in Menu directly

questions.tip: Mention Context as the built in solution and Redux/Zustand for bigger apps.

questions.question: What is useReducer and when should you use it?
questions.answer: useReducer manages state with a reducer function, similar to Redux but built into React. You send actions with dispatch and the reducer returns the new state. It is better than useState when the state is complex or when several values change together.
questions.tip: Rule of thumb: simple state uses useState, complex related state uses useReducer.

questions.question: What are custom hooks?
questions.answer: A custom hook is your own function that starts with "use" and reuses logic built from other hooks. It lets you share stateful logic between components without repeating code. It returns whatever you want, like values and functions.
questions.tip: The name must start with "use" or React's rules of hooks will not apply correctly.

questions.question: What are the rules of hooks?
questions.answer: Hooks must always be called at the top level of a component, never inside loops, conditions or nested functions. They can only be called from React function components or other custom hooks. This is because React tracks hooks by the order they are called.
questions.tip: Explain why: React relies on a consistent call order between renders.

questions.question: What is a controlled component?
questions.answer: A controlled component is a form input whose value is stored in React state and updated through onChange. React is the single source of truth for the value. This makes validation and resetting easy.

example.code:
const [email, setEmail] = useState("");
<input value={email} onChange={e => setEmail(e.target.value)} />

questions.tip: Controlled inputs are preferred — they keep the UI and state always in sync.

questions.question: What is an uncontrolled component?
questions.answer: An uncontrolled component lets the DOM keep the input value, and you read it with a ref when needed. There is no state and no onChange handler. It is useful for simple forms or file inputs.
questions.tip: Note that file inputs are always uncontrolled — a good practical detail to mention.

questions.question: How do you fetch data in React?
questions.answer: You usually call the API inside useEffect with an empty dependency array so it runs once on mount. You store the data, a loading flag and an error in state. In real projects, libraries like React Query or SWR handle caching and refetching for you.
questions.tip: Always handle loading and error states — interviewers check if you remember them.

questions.question: What are the component lifecycle phases in React?
questions.answer: The three phases are mounting when the component first appears, updating when props or state change, and unmounting when it is removed. In functional components, useEffect covers all three. The empty array runs on mount, dependencies run on update, and the return function runs on unmount.
questions.tip: Map class methods to useEffect: componentDidMount, componentDidUpdate and componentWillUnmount all in one hook.

questions.question: What is conditional rendering in React?
questions.answer: Conditional rendering means showing different UI based on a condition. You can use a ternary operator, the logical AND operator, or an early return. This is how you show loaders, empty states and error messages.

example.code:
{loading ? : } {error &&

Something went wrong

}

questions.tip: Be careful with the AND operator and numbers — zero will render as "0" on screen.

questions.question: How do you lift state up in React?
questions.answer: Lifting state up means moving state to the closest common parent when two components need to share it. The parent holds the state and passes the value and updater function down as props. This keeps both children in sync.
questions.tip: This is the standard answer for "how do two sibling components share data".

questions.question: What is a React fragment?
questions.answer: A fragment lets you return multiple elements from a component without adding an extra div to the DOM. You write it as empty angle brackets or React.Fragment. It keeps the HTML clean and avoids breaking CSS layouts like flex and grid.
questions.tip: Use React.Fragment with a key when rendering fragments inside a map.

questions.question: What is an error boundary?
questions.answer: An error boundary is a component that catches JavaScript errors in its child components and shows a fallback UI instead of crashing the whole app. It only works as a class component using componentDidCatch or getDerivedStateFromError. It does not catch errors in event handlers or async code.
questions.tip: Mention that this is one of the few things still requiring a class component.

questions.question: What is React Router and how does routing work?
questions.answer: React Router adds page navigation to a single page app without reloading the browser. You define routes that map a URL path to a component, and use Link instead of an anchor tag for navigation. The URL changes and React swaps the component.

example.code:
<BrowserRouter>
  <Routes>
    <Route path="/" element={<Home />} />
    <Route path="/user/:id" element={<User />} />
  </Routes>
</BrowserRouter>

questions.tip: Use useParams to read route parameters and useNavigate to redirect programmatically.

questions.question: What is lazy loading in React?
questions.answer: Lazy loading means loading a component only when it is actually needed, instead of in the first bundle. React.lazy with Suspense splits the code and shows a fallback while loading. This makes the initial page load much faster.

example.code:
const Dashboard = React.lazy(() => import("./Dashboard")); Loading...

}>

questions.tip: The proper term is "code splitting" — say it along with lazy loading.

questions.question: What is Redux and why is it used?
questions.answer: Redux is a state management library that keeps all shared app state in one central store. Components read from the store and send actions to change it through reducers. It is useful in large apps where many distant components need the same data.
questions.tip: Mention Redux Toolkit — plain Redux is considered outdated and too verbose now.

questions.question: When should you not use Redux?
questions.answer: You should not use Redux for small apps or for state that only one component needs. Local state with useState and shared state with Context are usually enough. Adding Redux too early makes simple features much harder to write.

example.code:
// Fine without Redux
const [isOpen, setIsOpen] = useState(false);

questions.tip: Saying "I only reach for Redux when Context is not enough" shows good judgement.

questions.question: What is the difference between Context API and Redux?
questions.answer: Context is built into React and is best for simple, rarely changing data like theme or user. Redux is a full library with a central store, devtools, middleware and better performance for frequently changing state. Context can re render many components if the value changes often.

example.code:
// Context: theme, language, auth user
// Redux: complex cart, filters, large shared data

questions.tip: The performance point about Context causing wide re renders is the detail interviewers want.

questions.question: How do you optimise performance in a React app?
questions.answer: Use React.memo, useMemo and useCallback to avoid unnecessary re renders, and give lists proper keys. Use lazy loading and code splitting to shrink the first bundle, and virtualise very long lists. Also avoid creating new objects or functions inline in props when it matters.

example.code:
const Row = React.memo(RowComponent);
const handle = useCallback(() => doThing(id), [id]);

questions.tip: Mention react-window or react-virtualized for rendering thousands of rows.

questions.question: What causes unnecessary re renders in React?
questions.answer: A component re renders when its state or props change, or when its parent re renders. Passing a new object, array or function created inline as a prop breaks memoisation because it is a new reference each time. Context value changes also re render every consumer.
questions.tip: The "new reference every render" point is the key insight here.

questions.question: What is the children prop?
questions.answer: children is a special prop that holds whatever you put between a component's opening and closing tags. It lets you build wrapper components like cards, modals and layouts. It makes components flexible and reusable.
questions.tip: This pattern is called composition — a strong word to use in interviews.

questions.question: What is the difference between state updates being batched or not?
questions.answer: Batching means React groups several state updates together and re renders only once, which is faster. Since React 18, updates are batched automatically everywhere, including inside promises and timeouts. Before React 18, only updates inside React event handlers were batched.
questions.tip: Mention "automatic batching in React 18" — it shows you know recent versions.

questions.question: What are React portals?
questions.answer: A portal renders a child component into a different part of the DOM, outside its parent. It is mainly used for modals, tooltips and dropdowns that must escape a parent with overflow hidden or a z-index problem. Events still bubble through the React tree as normal.

example.code: createPortal(<Modal />, document.getElementById("modal-root"));

questions.tip: Modals are the classic portal example — always mention them.

questions.question: How do you handle forms in React?
questions.answer: For simple forms you store each field in state and use controlled inputs with onChange. For bigger forms, libraries like React Hook Form reduce re renders and handle validation. Always call preventDefault on submit so the page does not reload.
questions.tip: Mention React Hook Form with Zod or Yup for validation — it is the common real world stack.

questions.question: What is StrictMode in React?
questions.answer: StrictMode is a development only wrapper that helps you find problems early. It intentionally runs some functions and effects twice in development to reveal unsafe side effects. It does nothing in production builds.

example.code:
<React.StrictMode>
  <App />
</React.StrictMode>

questions.tip: If someone asks "why does my useEffect run twice", the answer is StrictMode in development.

questions.question: What is the difference between client side rendering and server side rendering?
questions.answer: In client side rendering the browser downloads an almost empty HTML file and JavaScript builds the page, which is slower on first load and weaker for SEO. In server side rendering the server sends ready made HTML, so the page appears faster and search engines can read it. Next.js is the common way to get server rendering with React.

example.code:
// CSR: React builds the DOM in the browser
// SSR: server sends full HTML, React then hydrates it

questions.tip: Know the word "hydration": React attaching event handlers to server rendered HTML.

questions.question: How would you build a search with debounce in React?
questions.answer: You store the typed text in state and use a useEffect with a setTimeout that waits before calling the API. The cleanup function clears the timer whenever the text changes, so only the last pause triggers a request. This avoids one API call per keystroke.
questions.tip:
This is a very common practical React interview task — practise writing it from memory.

Next.jsRouting, Rendering, Server Components & SEO

questions.question: What is Next.js?
questions.answer: Next.js is a React framework that adds features React does not have on its own, like routing, server side rendering and API routes. It gives better performance and SEO out of the box. It is the most common way to build production React apps today.
questions.tip: Say React is a library and Next.js is the framework built on top of it.

questions.question: What are the main benefits of Next.js over plain React?
questions.answer: Next.js gives file based routing, server side rendering and static generation, image optimisation, API routes and automatic code splitting. These improve SEO and first load speed without extra setup. In plain React you would need to configure all of this yourself.

example.code:
// Routing is automatic from the folder structure
// app/about/page.js  ->  /about

questions.tip: The two biggest selling points to mention are SEO and performance.

questions.question: What is file based routing in Next.js?
questions.answer: In Next.js, your folder structure creates your routes automatically. A file at app/about/page.js becomes the /about URL, and no router configuration is needed. Nested folders create nested routes.
questions.tip: Know that square brackets in a folder name create a dynamic route.

questions.question: What is the difference between the Pages Router and the App Router?
questions.answer: The Pages Router is the older system using a pages folder, with getServerSideProps and getStaticProps for data. The App Router is the newer system using an app folder, with React Server Components, layouts and async components for data fetching. New projects should use the App Router.
questions.tip: Say the App Router is the current recommended approach and mention Server Components.

questions.question: What is SSR (Server Side Rendering) in Next.js?
questions.answer: SSR means the page HTML is generated on the server for every request. This is useful for pages with data that changes often or is user specific, like a dashboard. The user sees content faster and search engines can read the page.

example.code:
// App Router: no cache means render on every request
const res = await fetch(url, { cache: "no-store" });

questions.tip: SSR is for fresh, personalised data — mention dashboards and user profiles.

questions.question: What is SSG (Static Site Generation)?
questions.answer: SSG builds the HTML once at build time and serves the same file to everyone. It is extremely fast because the page is ready before any request comes in. It is best for content that rarely changes, like blogs, docs and marketing pages.

example.code:
// Default in App Router: cached at build time
const res = await fetch(url); // statically cached

questions.tip: Static pages are the fastest — say SSG whenever the content does not change per user.

questions.question: What is ISR (Incremental Static Regeneration)?
questions.answer: ISR lets a static page rebuild itself in the background after a set time, without rebuilding the whole site. Visitors get the fast static page, and it quietly updates when the time expires. It gives you static speed with fresh data.

example.code:
const res = await fetch(url, { next: { revalidate: 60 } });
// page refreshes at most once every 60 seconds

questions.tip: ISR is the "best of both worlds" answer between SSG and SSR.

questions.question: What is the difference between SSR, SSG, ISR and CSR?
questions.answer: CSR builds the page in the browser, SSR builds it on the server for every request, SSG builds it once at build time, and ISR is SSG that refreshes on a schedule. Choose CSR for private dashboards behind a login, SSR for fresh personalised data, and SSG or ISR for public content.
questions.tip: Be ready to give one real use case for each — that is what separates good answers.

questions.question: What are React Server Components in Next.js?
questions.answer: Server Components run only on the server and never send their JavaScript to the browser, which makes bundles smaller. They can fetch data and read from a database directly. They are the default in the App Router.
questions.tip: Server Components cannot use useState, useEffect or onClick — that needs a Client Component.

questions.question: What is the "use client" directive?
questions.answer: "use client" at the top of a file marks it as a Client Component, so it runs in the browser. You need it whenever you use hooks like useState or useEffect, or browser events like onClick. Everything else should stay a Server Component for better performance.
questions.tip: Best practice: keep "use client" as low in the tree as possible, on small leaf components.

questions.question: What are API routes in Next.js?
questions.answer: API routes let you write backend endpoints inside your Next.js project, so you do not need a separate server for simple tasks. In the App Router you create a route.js file and export functions named after HTTP methods. They run only on the server.
questions.tip: Mention that API routes are useful for hiding secret API keys from the browser.

questions.question: What is the next/image component?
questions.answer: next/image is an optimised image component that automatically resizes images, converts them to modern formats and lazy loads them. This greatly improves page speed and Core Web Vitals. It also prevents layout shift because you set width and height.

example.code:
import Image from "next/image";
<Image src="/photo.jpg" width={400} height={300} alt="Photo" />

questions.tip: Mention that it prevents layout shift (CLS) — a strong performance detail.

questions.question: What is the next/link component?
questions.answer: Link enables client side navigation between pages without a full page reload, which feels instant. Next.js also prefetches linked pages that are visible on screen. You should always use Link instead of a plain anchor tag for internal links.

example.code:
import Link from "next/link";
<Link href="/about">About</Link>

questions.tip: Prefetching is the key benefit to mention — it makes navigation feel instant.

questions.question: What are layouts in the Next.js App Router?
questions.answer: A layout is shared UI, like a navbar or sidebar, that wraps multiple pages. It is defined in a layout.js file and applies to everything inside that folder. Layouts keep their state and do not re render when you navigate between child pages.
questions.tip: The fact that layouts preserve state across navigation is a nice detail to add.

questions.question: What are loading.js and error.js in Next.js?
questions.answer: loading.js automatically shows a loading UI while a page or its data is being prepared, using React Suspense behind the scenes. error.js catches errors in that route segment and shows a fallback instead of crashing. Both are placed in the same folder as the page.
questions.tip: These files remove a lot of manual loading and error state code — mention that benefit.

questions.question: How do you handle dynamic routes and route parameters in Next.js?
questions.answer: You create a folder with the name in square brackets, like [id], and Next.js treats it as a dynamic segment. In a Server Component the value comes in through the params prop. Catch all routes use three dots inside the brackets.
