questions.tip: Know the three types: [id] dynamic, [...slug] catch all, and [[...slug]] optional catch all.

questions.question: What are environment variables in Next.js?
questions.answer: Environment variables store secrets and settings outside your code in a .env.local file. By default they are only available on the server, which keeps them safe. If a variable must be used in the browser, its name must start with NEXT_PUBLIC_.
questions.tip: Never put a secret in a NEXT_PUBLIC_ variable — it will be visible in the browser.

questions.question: What is middleware in Next.js?
questions.answer: Middleware runs before a request finishes, so you can redirect, rewrite or block it. It is commonly used for authentication checks, redirects and localisation. It lives in a middleware.js file at the project root and runs on the edge, before the page loads.
questions.tip: Protecting routes for logged out users is the classic middleware example.

questions.question: How does Next.js improve SEO?
questions.answer: Next.js sends ready made HTML from the server, so search engine crawlers can read the content immediately, unlike plain client rendered React. It also supports metadata for titles and descriptions, automatic sitemaps and fast page speed, which is an SEO ranking factor. Image and font optimisation improve Core Web Vitals too.
questions.tip: The core point: HTML is ready on the server, so crawlers do not need to run JavaScript.

questions.question: How would you handle authentication in a Next.js app?
questions.answer: A common approach is to log the user in through an API route, then store a token in an HTTP only cookie so JavaScript cannot read it. Middleware checks that cookie and redirects logged out users away from protected pages. Libraries like NextAuth or Auth.js handle most of this for you.

example.code:
// middleware.js protects the dashboard
export const config = { matcher: ["/dashboard/:path*"] };

questions.tip:
HTTP only cookies are safer than localStorage for tokens because they resist XSS attacks.

TypeScriptTypes, Generics, Utility Types & React Typing

questions.question: What is TypeScript?
questions.answer: TypeScript is JavaScript with types added on top. It catches mistakes while you are writing code instead of when the app is running. Browsers cannot run it directly, so it is compiled into plain JavaScript.

example.code:
let name: string = "Umyma";
name = 5; // Error caught before running

questions.tip: Say TypeScript is a "superset of JavaScript" — every valid JS file is valid TS.

questions.question: What are the benefits of using TypeScript?
questions.answer: It catches bugs early, gives much better autocomplete in the editor, and makes large codebases easier to refactor. Types also act as documentation, so other developers understand what a function expects. The main cost is extra setup and slightly more code to write.
questions.tip: Mention autocomplete and safe refactoring — those are the benefits teams care about most.

questions.question: What are the basic types in TypeScript?
questions.answer: The common types are string, number, boolean, null, undefined, array, object, any, unknown, void and never. Arrays are written with square brackets after the type. TypeScript can also guess the type automatically, which is called inference.
questions.tip: Mention type inference: you do not always need to write the type explicitly.

questions.question: What is the difference between any, unknown and never?
questions.answer: any turns off type checking completely and should be avoided. unknown is the safe version: you can assign anything to it, but you must check the type before using it. never means a value that can never happen, like a function that always throws an error.
questions.tip: Saying "I use unknown instead of any" shows strong TypeScript discipline.

questions.question: What is the difference between type and interface?
questions.answer: Both describe the shape of an object. interface can be reopened and extended later, and is usually preferred for object shapes. type is more flexible and can also describe unions, intersections and primitives.
questions.tip: Simple rule: interface for object shapes, type for unions and everything else.

questions.question: What are union and intersection types?
questions.answer: A union with the pipe symbol means the value can be one of several types. An intersection with the ampersand combines several types into one that has all the properties. Unions are very common for things like status values.
questions.tip: Remember: pipe means "or", ampersand means "and".

questions.question: What are optional and readonly properties?
questions.answer: A question mark after a property name makes it optional, so it may be missing. readonly means the property can be set once but never changed afterwards. Both help describe data shapes accurately.
questions.tip: Optional properties become type "undefined or the type", so you must check before using them.

questions.question: What are generics in TypeScript?
questions.answer: Generics let you write a function or type that works with many types while keeping type safety. You use a placeholder like T that is filled in when the function is used. This avoids using any and losing type information.
questions.tip: Generics are the most asked intermediate TypeScript question — practise a simple example.

questions.question: What is an enum in TypeScript?
questions.answer: An enum is a set of named constant values, useful for fixed options like roles or statuses. By default the values are numbers starting at zero, but you can set string values instead. Many teams now prefer union types over enums because they are simpler.
questions.tip: Mention that string union types are often preferred over enums in modern TypeScript.

questions.question: What is type assertion?
questions.answer: Type assertion tells TypeScript to treat a value as a specific type when you know more than the compiler does. It is written with the "as" keyword. It does not change the value at runtime, so an incorrect assertion can cause bugs.

example.code:
const input = document.getElementById("email") as HTMLInputElement;
console.log(input.value);

questions.tip: Say assertions should be rare — they bypass type safety, so prefer proper typing.

questions.question: What is type narrowing?
questions.answer: Narrowing is when TypeScript figures out a more specific type inside a condition. Checks like typeof, instanceof, or checking if a property exists all narrow the type. This lets you safely use type specific methods.
questions.tip: Narrowing is how you safely work with union types — always pair the two concepts.

questions.question: What are utility types like Partial, Pick and Omit?
questions.answer: Utility types build new types from existing ones without repeating code. Partial makes all properties optional, Required makes them all required, Pick keeps only chosen properties, and Omit removes chosen ones. Record builds an object type from a key type and a value type.
questions.tip: Partial is extremely common for update functions — mention that use case.

questions.question: How do you type a function in TypeScript?
questions.answer: You add types to the parameters and after the parentheses for the return value. You can also define a reusable function type separately. If a function returns nothing, its return type is void.
questions.tip: Return types are often inferred, but writing them explicitly makes public APIs clearer.

questions.question: How do you type React props with TypeScript?
questions.answer: You define an interface or type describing the props, then use it on the component's parameter. Optional props get a question mark, and children are typed as React.ReactNode. This gives autocomplete and errors when a prop is missing.
questions.tip: This is the most practical TypeScript question for a frontend role — be ready to write it.

questions.question: How do you type useState and useRef in React?
questions.answer: useState usually infers the type from the initial value, but you pass a generic when the value can be null or a union. useRef for a DOM element is typed with the element type and null, then accessed through current. Always handle the possibility that current is null.
questions.tip: The useState<Type | null>(null) pattern is extremely common for API data.

questions.question: What is the difference between unknown and any when handling API data?
questions.answer: If you type API data as any, TypeScript gives you no protection and typos slip through silently. If you type it as unknown, you are forced to check or validate the shape before using it. Many teams use a validation library like Zod to turn unknown data into a trusted type.
questions.tip: Mentioning Zod or runtime validation shows real world TypeScript experience.

questions.question: What are literal types?
questions.answer: A literal type restricts a value to exact specific values instead of any string or number. They are usually combined into a union to model fixed options. This catches typos that a plain string type would allow.
questions.tip: Literal unions are the modern replacement for enums in most frontend code.

questions.question: What is the non null assertion operator?
questions.answer: An exclamation mark after a value tells TypeScript that it is definitely not null or undefined. It removes the error but does not actually check anything at runtime, so it can still crash. Optional chaining is usually safer.
questions.tip: Say you prefer optional chaining or a proper null check over the exclamation mark.

questions.question: What is the tsconfig file and what is strict mode?
questions.answer: tsconfig.json holds the TypeScript compiler settings for a project, like which files to include and how strict to be. Turning on strict enables several safety checks together, such as strictNullChecks, which forces you to handle null and undefined. New projects should always use strict mode.
questions.tip: Mention strictNullChecks specifically — it is the setting that prevents the most bugs.

questions.question: What is the difference between compile time and runtime in TypeScript?
questions.answer: TypeScript types only exist while you are writing and compiling code, and they are completely removed from the final JavaScript. This means types cannot check data that arrives at runtime, like an API response. For runtime safety you need actual checks or a validation library.

example.code:
interface User { name: string }
// After compiling, no type information remains in the JS output

questions.tip: The phrase "types are erased at compile time" is exactly what interviewers want to hear.

questions.question: What is React?
questions.answer:
React is a JavaScript library for building user interfaces, especially component-based and interactive web applications. It allows us to break the UI into reusable components and efficiently update the UI when state or props change. What is a component? A component is a reusable piece of UI. function UserCard({ name }) { return

{name}

; } Components can have: - Props - State - Event handlers - Hooks - Child components

questions.question: What are props?
What are the main React Hooks and when should you use them?
questions.answer:
Hooks allow functional components to use React features such as state and effects. useState Ans: useState is a React Hook that allows a functional component to store and manage local state. When the state setter is called with a new value, React schedules a re-render so the UI can reflect the updated state. Syntax const [state, setState] = useState(initialValue); Example: function Counter() { const [count, setCount] = useState(0); return ( ); } Here: count -> current state setCount -> function used to update state 0 -> initial value Updating based on previous state If the new state depends on the previous state, use the functional updater: setCount(prevCount => prevCount + 1); This is especially important when multiple updates may be queued. setCount(prev => prev + 1); setCount(prev => prev + 1); The state increases by 2. useState is used to manage local state in functional components. It returns the current state value and a setter function. Calling the setter schedules a re-render. When the next state depends on the previous state, I use the functional updater form to ensure I work with the latest state. 2. useEffect useEffect is used to synchronize a component with external systems. Examples include: - API requests - Timers - Event listeners - WebSocket subscriptions - Browser APIs - Third-party libraries useEffect(() => { // side effect }, []); Dependency array No dependency array useEffect(() => { console.log("Effect"); }); Runs after every completed render. Empty dependency array useEffect(() => { console.log("Effect"); }, []); Runs after the initial mount in normal production behavior. In development with React Strict Mode, React may intentionally run setup/cleanup an extra time to help identify unsafe effects. With dependencies useEffect(() => { fetchUser(userId); }, [userId]); The effect runs after the initial render and again when userId changes. Cleanup An effect can return a cleanup function: useEffect(() => { const timer = setInterval(() => { console.log("Running"); }, 1000); return () => { clearInterval(timer); }; }, []); Cleanup happens when the component is removed and before the effect is re-run because dependencies changed. API example useEffect(() => { const fetchUsers = async () => { const response = await fetch("/api/users"); const data = await response.json(); setUsers(data); }; fetchUsers(); }, []); In production applications, you should also consider: - loading state - error handling - cancellation - caching - race conditions Interview answer useEffect is used to synchronize a component with external systems such as APIs, subscriptions, timers, browser APIs, or third-party libraries. The dependency array controls when the effect is re-synchronized, and the cleanup function is used to remove subscriptions, timers, listeners, or other resources. 3. useContext useContext allows a component to read a value from React Context without manually passing that value through every intermediate component. Without Context: App -> Parent -> Child -> GrandChild You may have to pass props through every level. This is called prop drilling. Context can provide the value directly to consumers. Example Create context: const ThemeContext = createContext(null); Provide value: Consume it: const theme = useContext(ThemeContext); Common use cases - Theme - Authentication/user information - Language - Application configuration Important interview point Context is not automatically a replacement for Redux. Context is a mechanism for passing values through the tree. Redux and other state-management libraries provide additional patterns and tooling for managing complex application state. 4. useReducer useReducer is useful for managing complex state logic, especially when state updates involve multiple actions or related pieces of state. It works similarly to the reducer concept used in Redux. Syntax const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, initialState); Example: function reducer(state, action) { switch (action.type) { case "increment": return { ...state, count: state.count + 1 }; case "decrement": return { ...state, count: state.count - 1 }; default: return state; } } Component: function Counter() { const [state, dispatch] = useReducer(reducer, { count: 0 }); return ( <>

{state.count}

); } Flow: User action -> dispatch() -> Action -> Reducer -> New State -> Re-render When should you use it? Use useReducer when: - State has multiple related fields - There are many state transitions - State update logic is becoming complicated - You want explicit actions For simple state: const [count, setCount] = useState(0); is usually easier. 5. useRef useRef creates a mutable object whose .current property persists across renders without causing a re-render when changed. const ref = useRef(initialValue); DOM access One common use case is accessing a DOM element: function Input() { const inputRef = useRef(null); const focusInput = () => { inputRef.current.focus(); }; return ( <> ); } Storing values between renders You can also use it for mutable values: const renderCount = useRef(0); renderCount.current += 1; Changing: renderCount.current doesn't itself trigger a re-render. useState vs useRef useState useRef Stores state Stores mutable reference Updating causes re-render Updating .current doesn't cause re-render Used for UI state DOM references / persistent mutable values Interview answer I use useRef when I need a value to persist across renders without triggering a re-render, or when I need to access a DOM element directly. 6. useMemo Ans: useMemo memoizes the result of a calculation. const value = useMemo(() => { return expensiveCalculation(data); }, [data]); React can reuse the previously calculated value until a dependency changes. Example const filteredUsers = useMemo(() => { return users.filter(user => user.active); }, [users]); If another state changes but users doesn't, React can reuse the memoized result. Important Don't use useMemo everywhere. This: const total = useMemo(() => price * quantity, [price, quantity]); may provide no meaningful benefit if the calculation is trivial. Interview answer useMemo is used to memoize the result of an expensive calculation so React can reuse the previous result when its dependencies haven't changed. I use it when profiling or the calculation/reference behavior justifies it, rather than using it for every value. 7. useCallback useCallback memoizes a function reference. const handleClick = useCallback(() => { console.log("Clicked"); }, []); This is particularly useful when passing callbacks to memoized child components. Why? Every render normally creates a new function: function Parent() { const handleClick = () => { console.log("Hello"); }; return ; } Conceptually: Render 1 -> Function A Render 2 -> Function B Render 3 -> Function C Even though the function looks identical: Function A !== Function B With useCallback: const handleClick = useCallback(() => { console.log("Hello"); }, []); React can preserve the function identity while dependencies remain unchanged. useMemo vs useCallback This is a very common interview question. useMemo -> memoizes a value useCallback -> memoizes a function Example: const result = useMemo(() => calculate(), [data]); const handleClick = useCallback(() => { doSomething(); }, []); 8. useLayoutEffect useLayoutEffect is similar to useEffect, but its effect runs synchronously after DOM mutations and before the browser paints the updated screen. This makes it useful when you need to: - Measure DOM dimensions - Read layout information - Make a DOM adjustment before the user sees the result Example: useLayoutEffect(() => { const width = elementRef.current.getBoundingClientRect().width; console.log(width); }, []); Difference useEffect DOM update -> Browser may paint -> Effect useLayoutEffect DOM update -> Layout effect -> Browser paint Because useLayoutEffect can block painting, don't use it for ordinary effects when useEffect is sufficient.

questions.question: How do re-rendering and reconciliation work in React?
questions.answer:
1. What causes a React component to re-render? Main causes: 1. Its state changes 2. Its props change 3. Its parent re-renders 4. A consumed context value changes

Example:

const [count, setCount] = useState(0);

setCount(count + 1); The state update causes React to render the component again. Does re-render mean the DOM is recreated? No. React calculates what changed and updates only the necessary parts of the actual DOM. What is reconciliation? Reconciliation is the process React uses to compare the previous UI representation with the new one and determine what needs to be updated. Keys are particularly important when rendering lists. users.map(user => ( <UserCard key={user.id} user={user} /> )) A stable key helps React correctly identify elements between renders.

2. Virtual DOM & React Fiber What is Virtual DOM? The Virtual DOM is a lightweight in-memory representation of the UI that React uses to determine what changes need to be made to the actual DOM. For example: State changes -> React renders -> New UI representation -> Compare with previous -> Determine changes -> Update DOM

3. What is React Fiber? Fiber is React's internal reconciliation architecture. It represents work as units that React can schedule and prioritize, enabling more sophisticated rendering behavior. It helps React handle rendering work more efficiently and supports capabilities such as concurrent rendering. Interview tip Don't say: "Virtual DOM makes React automatically faster than every other framework." Instead: "React's reconciliation and scheduling mechanisms help minimize unnecessary DOM work and manage rendering efficiently."

questions.question: How do props, state, and Context differ?

Props vs State Props State Passed by parent Managed by component Read-only Can be updated Used to configure component Represents changing data Changes when parent provides new value Changes through state updates Example: function User({ name }) { const [age, setAge] = useState(25); return ( <>

{name}

Good examples: - Theme - Authentication/user information - Language - Configuration Avoid putting every piece of application state into Context because context updates can cause consumers to re-render.

Bundle optimization

Strong interview answer I don't use memoization everywhere. I first profile the application, identify unnecessary renders or expensive operations, and then apply techniques such as React.memo, useMemo, useCallback, code splitting, lazy loading, image optimization, caching, and list virtualization where they actually provide a benefit.

questions.question: How should state be managed in React?
questions.answer:
State management means managing application data that changes over time. Local state Use: useState() for state needed by one component or a small component tree. Context Useful for relatively global values: Theme User Language Redux Useful when an application has complex global state and predictable state transitions.

Example architecture

Component -> Action -> Reducer ->

Store -> Component Redux vs Context Context is primarily a mechanism for passing values through the component tree. Redux is a state management solution with a structured architecture for managing complex application state. Don't say: "Redux is always better." Choose based on the application's requirements.

questions.question: How do you integrate APIs in React?
What React performance and best practices should you follow?
questions.answer:
These overlap with optimization, but interviewers may ask for best practices separately. Component design Keep components:

- Small

- Reusable

- Focused

- Easy to understand

Avoid huge components containing everything. Use meaningful names Instead of: <Cmp /> use: <UserProfile /> Don't duplicate logic Extract repeated logic into:

- Custom hooks

- Utility functions

- Reusable components

Don't overuse global state Keep state as close as possible to where it is needed. Don't overuse useMemo / useCallback They aren't automatically performance improvements. Use them when reference stability or expensive computation makes them worthwhile. Use stable keys Good: users.map(user => ( <User key={user.id} user={user} /> )) Avoid using array index as key when list ordering can change. Handle loading/error states Don't assume APIs always succeed. Keep secrets out of frontend code Never expose sensitive credentials or private API keys in client-side JavaScript.

questions.question: How would you design a React application?
questions.answer: For a medium-sized application, I might structure it like: src/ │ ├── components/ │ ├── common/ │ └── features/ │ ├── pages/ or app/ │ ├── hooks/ │ ├── services/ │ ├── utils/ │ ├── types/ │ ├── store/ │ └── styles/ And conceptually: UI -> Components -> Hooks / State -> Services -> REST API -> Backend -> Database

Ans: Keys are unique identifiers that React uses to identify elements in a list. They help React understand which items were added, removed, or changed when the list is updated. Keys are mainly used when rendering lists using .map(). Example const users = [ { id: 1, name: "Avhi" }, { id: 2, name: "Rahul" }, { id: 3, name: "Amit" } ]; function Users() { return (
{users.map(user => (
{user.name}
))}
); } Here: key={user.id} uniquely identifies each item. How does it work? Suppose initially React has: 1 -> Avhi 2 -> Rahul 3 -> Amit Then the data changes to: 1 -> Avhi 3 -> Amit 4 -> John Because React has keys: 1 -> same item 3 -> same item 2 -> removed 4 -> new item React can efficiently determine what changed instead of treating the entire list as completely new. Why shouldn't we normally use array index? // Avoid when list can change users.map((user, index) => ( )); If items are inserted, removed, or reordered, indexes can change and React may associate the wrong component/state with an item. I prefer using a stable unique ID from the data, such as user.id, instead of the array index, especially when the list can be reordered or modified.

questions.answer:
Ans: A Higher-Order Component, or HOC, is a function that takes a React component as input and returns a new enhanced component. The basic pattern is: const EnhancedComponent = HOC(OriginalComponent); Think of it as: Component -> HOC -> Enhanced Component Simple Example function withLoading(Component) { return function EnhancedComponent({ loading, ...props }) { if (loading) { return

Loading...

Historically, HOCs were commonly used to reuse component behavior such as: - Authentication - Permissions - Loading states - Logging - Feature flags - Data subscriptions For example: UserComponent -> withAuthentication() -> ProtectedUserComponent HOC vs Custom Hook This is important for modern React. For new functional-component code, custom Hooks are often a cleaner way to reuse logic. HOC withAuth(UserProfile) Enhances a component. Custom Hook const { user } = useAuth(); Shares logic directly inside the component. Interview Answer A Higher-Order Component is a function that takes a component and returns an enhanced component. It was commonly used to reuse cross-cutting component logic such as authentication, permissions, or loading behavior. In modern functional React applications, I would usually prefer custom Hooks for sharing logic because they are generally simpler and avoid adding extra component layers.

questions.question: What are the phases of the component lifecycle?
questions.answer:
A React component lifecycle can be understood in three main phases: Mounting -> Updating -> Unmounting 1. Mounting Mounting means the component is being added to the UI for the first time. Example: function User() { useEffect(() => { console.log("Component mounted"); }, []); return

User

; } The component renders and then the effect runs. Typical activities: - Initial rendering - Setting up subscriptions - Initial data fetching - Setting up event listeners 2. Updating Updating happens when something that affects the component changes. For example: - State changes - Props change - Consumed context changes const [count, setCount] = useState(0); When: setCount(1); React renders again. An effect with dependencies can respond to the change: useEffect(() => { console.log("count changed"); }, [count]); 3. Unmounting Unmounting means the component is removed from the UI. This is where cleanup is important. useEffect(() => { const timer = setInterval(() => { console.log("Running"); }, 1000); return () => { clearInterval(timer); }; }, []); When the component is removed, the cleanup function runs. Real-time example Suppose you have a chat component: Open Chat -> Connect WebSocket -> User interacts -> Component updates -> Close Chat -> Disconnect WebSocket The connection should be cleaned up when the component unmounts. Interview Answer A React component lifecycle can be understood in three phases: mounting, updating, and unmounting. During mounting, the component is created and rendered. During updating, React re- renders when relevant state, props, or context changes. During unmounting, the component is removed from the UI and we should clean up resources such as subscriptions, timers, and event listeners. With functional components, useEffect and its cleanup function are commonly used for this synchronization and cleanup.

questions.question: How do React Suspense and React.lazy enable code splitting?
questions.answer:
What is Code Splitting? Code splitting means breaking the application's JavaScript bundle into smaller chunks and loading them when they are needed instead of loading everything initially. Without code splitting: Application -> Huge JS Bundle -> Browser downloads everything With code splitting: Application -> ┌──────┬──────┬──────┐ Home Admin Reports -> -> -> load load load when when when needed needed needed This can improve initial loading performance. React.lazy React.lazy allows you to dynamically import a component. const Dashboard = React.lazy( () => import("./Dashboard") ); The Dashboard code doesn't need to be included in the initial JavaScript execution path in the same way as a normal static import. Suspense Suspense lets you specify a fallback UI while something is waiting. Loading...

}> Complete example: import { lazy, Suspense } from "react"; const Dashboard = lazy( () => import("./Dashboard") ); function App() { return ( Loading...

}> ); } How they work together User needs Dashboard -> React.lazy() -> Dynamic import() -> Dashboard chunk requested -> Suspense shows fallback -> Chunk loads -> Dashboard renders Real-time example Imagine an admin application: Login -> Dashboard -> Reports -> Analytics -> Settings A normal user may never open: Reports Analytics Settings There is little reason to make all of those feature modules part of the initial loading path. You can lazy-load them: const Reports = lazy(() => import("./Reports")); const Analytics = lazy(() => import("./Analytics")); Then load them when the user navigates to those sections. Important interview point Suspense itself doesn't perform code splitting. React.lazy + dynamic import enables component-level code splitting, while Suspense provides the fallback UI while the lazy component is loading. Interview Answer Code splitting means dividing the application's JavaScript into smaller chunks so that we don't have to load everything upfront. React.lazy allows us to dynamically import a component, and Suspense provides a fallback UI while that component is loading. For example, in an admin application I can lazy-load Reports or Analytics pages so their code is fetched when the user actually needs them, reducing the initial JavaScript required by the application.

questions.question: What router types are used in React?
questions.answer:
In React, routing is commonly handled using React Router. It allows us to display different components based on the URL without doing a full page reload. Main types/patterns 1. BrowserRouter Uses the browser's History API and normal-looking URLs. import { BrowserRouter } from "react-router-dom";

<BrowserRouter> <App /> </BrowserRouter>

Example URLs:

/ -> Home /about -> About /products -> Products This is the most commonly used router for standard web applications.

2. HashRouter Uses the URL hash (#) for routing. import { HashRouter } from "react-router-dom";

<HashRouter> <App /> </HashRouter> URLs look like: /#/ /#/about /#/products It's useful when server-side configuration for SPA routes isn't available, because everything after # isn't sent to the server as part of the request path.

3. MemoryRouter Keeps routing information in memory instead of the browser URL. import { MemoryRouter } from "react-router-dom";

<MemoryRouter> <App /> </MemoryRouter> It's mainly useful for:

- Testing

- Non-browser environments

- Specialized embedded applications

What about createBrowserRouter? Modern React Router also provides data routers, such as: createBrowserRouter() createHashRouter() createMemoryRouter() For example: const router = createBrowserRouter([ { path: "/", element: <Home /> }, { path: "/about", element: <About /> } ]); Interview Answer React itself doesn't provide routing; we commonly use React Router. The main router types are BrowserRouter, HashRouter, and MemoryRouter. BrowserRouter is commonly used for web applications and uses the browser History API, HashRouter uses the URL hash, and MemoryRouter keeps the routing state in memory and is commonly useful for testing or non-browser environments. Modern React Router also provides data-router APIs such as createBrowserRouter.

questions.question: A click handler calls setCount(count + 1) three times. Why does the count usually increase by one, and how do you make it increase by three?
questions.answer: Each render gives the handler one fixed snapshot of count. All three calls request the same next value. Pass updater functions instead: setCount(c => c + 1) three times. React queues them and gives each updater the result of the previous updater.
questions.tip: Say “state snapshot” and “updater queue.” Do not explain it as setState being slow.

questions.question: Why can a timeout created in a React event handler read an old state value even after the screen has updated?
questions.answer: The timeout callback closes over the state snapshot from the render that created the handler. A later render creates new variables and handlers, but it does not change the old closure. Pass the needed value, use an updater when changing state, or use a ref only when the callback truly needs the latest mutable value.
questions.tip: A stale value is often correct snapshot behavior. Explain the desired timing before choosing a fix.

questions.question: A reorderable list uses array indexes as keys. Why can text typed into one row appear in another row after sorting?
questions.answer: Keys tell React which item owns a component instance and its state. An index describes a position, so sorting can connect the old state at position 0 to a different item now at position 0. Use a stable ID from the data.
questions.tip: Mention identity and preserved state, not only rendering performance.

questions.question: How can a key intentionally reset a form, and when is that useful?
questions.answer: React preserves state for the same component type, key, and position. Changing the key gives the subtree a new identity, so React removes the old instance and creates fresh state. This is useful when switching records such as chat recipients or draft editors that must not share local form state.
questions.tip: Do not generate a random key on every render. That would reset the component every time.

questions.question: A component mutates an object in state and passes the same object back to the setter. Why may React skip the expected update?
questions.answer: React treats state as a snapshot and compares the new value with the old one using Object.is. Mutating the old object keeps the same reference, so React may see no state change. Create a new object and copy the fields that should remain.

example.code: setUser(current => ({ ...current, name: 'Mina' }));

questions.tip: Also explain that mutation changes earlier snapshots and makes debugging harder.

questions.question: Why can a component render twice and an Effect run setup, cleanup, and setup again in development Strict Mode?
questions.answer: Strict Mode runs extra development-only checks to expose impure rendering and missing Effect cleanup. Production does not keep the extra development cycle. Fix the impurity or cleanup instead of adding a flag that hides the second run.
questions.tip: A strong answer explains what bug the extra run reveals.

questions.question: An Effect reads a prop but the dependency array is empty. What bug can this create?
questions.answer: The Effect keeps the values from the render when it was created and will not re-synchronize when that prop changes. This can create stale subscriptions, requests, or timers. Include every reactive value used by the Effect, or restructure the code so the value is no longer reactive.
questions.tip: Do not disable the Hooks linter as the first fix.

questions.question: A user changes search terms quickly and an older fetch response replaces the newer result. How would you prevent that race?
questions.answer: The Effect cleanup should mark the old request as irrelevant or abort it. Only the latest active request may update state. Cleanup runs before the Effect re-runs and when the component unmounts.
questions.tip: Mention AbortController when the API supports cancellation, and still reason about stale responses.

questions.question: When is useLayoutEffect justified instead of useEffect?
questions.answer: Use useLayoutEffect when code must measure layout or make a visual correction before the browser paints, such as positioning a tooltip from its measured size. It blocks painting, so normal synchronization and data work should use useEffect.
questions.tip: Give a visual measurement example and mention the performance cost.

questions.question: Why can useMemo fail to help when one dependency is a new object created during every render?
questions.answer: React compares dependencies with Object.is. A freshly created object has a new identity on every render, so the memo recalculates. Move object creation inside the memo calculation, memoize the object for a real reason, or depend on stable primitive values.
questions.tip: Memoization is a performance tool. The code must remain correct without it.

questions.question: Why can one large Context make many unrelated consumers re-render, and how can you reduce that work?
questions.answer: When the provider value changes identity, consumers reading that context re-render. Split unrelated data into smaller contexts, keep provider values stable when useful, place providers close to their consumers, and measure before adding memoization. External stores with selectors may help for high-frequency shared state.
questions.tip: Do not claim React.memo blocks a changed context value; the consumer still receives the new context.

questions.question: What causes a hydration mismatch, and why is suppressHydrationWarning not a general fix?
questions.answer: Hydration expects the client’s first render to match the server HTML. Time-dependent values, random output, browser-only branches, invalid nesting, or different data can break that contract. Fix the deterministic render or move client-only differences after hydration. The warning suppression is an escape hatch for a known unavoidable text or attribute difference and does not repair mismatched logic.
questions.tip: Explain how you would make the first server and client output deterministic.

questions.question: What is the output order of synchronous logs, Promise callbacks, and setTimeout callbacks?
questions.answer: The current job runs first. After its stack becomes empty, queued microtasks such as Promise reactions run before the next task such as a timer callback. For console.log("A"); setTimeout(() => console.log("T")); Promise.resolve().then(() => console.log("P")); console.log("B"); the usual order is A, B, P, T.
questions.tip: Say the exact queues and do not use “async always runs later” as the explanation.

questions.question: Why do callbacks created in a for loop with var often see the final index, while let gives each iteration its own value?
questions.answer: Closures capture bindings, not frozen copies. var creates one function-scoped binding shared by every callback. let in a for loop creates a new per-iteration binding, so each callback closes over a different value.
questions.tip: Connect the answer to lexical scope and closures.

questions.question: How does this differ between an arrow function and a regular function?
questions.answer: A regular function receives this from how it is called: as a method, constructor, or through call/apply/bind. An arrow function has no own this and reads it lexically from the surrounding scope. That makes arrows useful for callbacks but unsuitable when a method needs a dynamic receiver or when a constructor is required.
questions.tip: Use a call-site example. Avoid saying this points to the function itself.

questions.question: What important values behave differently with === and Object.is?
questions.answer: Both avoid type coercion, but Object.is treats NaN as equal to itself and treats +0 and -0 as different. Strict equality treats NaN as unequal to itself and +0 as equal to -0. React uses Object.is for many state and dependency comparisons.
questions.tip: Know the edge cases; do not confuse Object.is with deep equality.

questions.question: Why does spreading an object not protect nested objects from mutation?
questions.answer: Object spread creates a shallow copy. The top-level object is new, but nested object and array references are reused. Mutating a reused nested value also changes what the old object sees. Copy every changed level or use a tool that produces immutable updates.
questions.tip: Draw the references if the interviewer asks why.

questions.question: What is the difference between debounce and throttle, and where would you use each?
questions.answer: Debounce waits until calls stop for a period, so it fits search input or autosave after typing pauses. Throttle limits execution to at most once per interval, so it fits scroll or pointer updates that still need periodic progress. Both must define leading/trailing behavior and cleanup pending timers.
questions.tip: Discuss user experience and cancellation, not only the timer code.

questions.question: How does Promise.all behave when one input rejects, and when is Promise.allSettled a better choice?
questions.answer: Promise.all fulfills when every input fulfills and rejects as soon as one input rejects. The other operations are not automatically cancelled. Promise.allSettled waits for every input and reports each status, which is useful when partial results or a full error report matter.
questions.tip: Mention cancellation separately; Promise.all does not cancel fetches for you.

questions.question: How does event delegation handle many dynamic child elements with one listener?
questions.answer: Place one listener on a stable ancestor and use event.target.closest() to find the relevant descendant. Bubbling lets the ancestor receive the event even for children added later. Verify that the matched element belongs to the intended container.
questions.tip: Mention that focus and some other events have different bubbling behavior or alternatives.

questions.question: How does property lookup work through the prototype chain, and what does shadowing mean?
questions.answer: JavaScript first checks an object’s own property. If it is absent, lookup follows the object’s prototype and continues until a match or null. An own property with the same name shadows the inherited property without changing the prototype.
questions.tip: Distinguish instance data, prototype methods, and class syntax sugar.

questions.question: Can a long chain of microtasks delay rendering or timers?
questions.answer: Yes. After a task finishes, the event loop drains the microtask queue before moving to rendering and the next task. If each microtask queues another microtask, other work can be delayed. Break large work into tasks or scheduled chunks when the browser needs chances to paint and respond.
questions.tip: This is a useful follow-up to the normal Promise-before-timer question.

questions.question: What is the difference between event capturing and bubbling, and how does stopPropagation affect them?
questions.answer: An event travels from the outer document toward the target during capture, reaches the target, then normally travels back through ancestors during bubbling. A listener can opt into capture. stopPropagation prevents further travel after it is called, but it does not cancel the browser’s default action; preventDefault handles that when allowed.
questions.tip: Explain the phases before recommending stopPropagation, because it can break shared behavior.

questions.question: What makes a custom modal dialog accessible beyond adding role="dialog"?
questions.answer: Give it an accessible name, move focus inside when it opens, keep keyboard focus within the modal while active, close on an expected action such as Escape, make background content unavailable, and restore focus to the opener. Prefer the native dialog element when it fits, but still test focus and labeling.
questions.tip: Accessibility is behavior plus semantics. A role alone is incomplete.

questions.question: When should you use native HTML instead of adding an ARIA role?
questions.answer: Use the native element when it provides the required meaning and behavior, such as button, nav, input, or details. Native controls include keyboard behavior, form behavior, and accessibility mappings. ARIA can describe missing semantics, but it does not automatically add interaction behavior.
questions.tip: A div with role="button" still needs keyboard activation and focus behavior.

questions.question: What triggers a CORS preflight request, and what does the browser check?
questions.answer: For a cross-origin request that is not a CORS-safelisted request, the browser first sends OPTIONS with the intended method and headers. The server must allow the origin, method, and requested headers in its response. CORS is enforced by browsers; it is not authentication and does not stop non-browser clients from sending requests.
questions.tip: Mention credentials rules separately because wildcard origins cannot be used with credentialed requests.

questions.question: How would you reduce XSS risk when rendering user-provided content in a React application?
questions.answer: Render untrusted text through normal JSX so React escapes it. Avoid dangerouslySetInnerHTML. If trusted product requirements need HTML, sanitize it with a maintained allowlist-based sanitizer before rendering, apply a Content Security Policy as another layer, and never treat client-side validation as the security boundary.
questions.tip: Sanitization and output encoding depend on the output context.

questions.question: What happens from entering a URL until a page becomes interactive, and where would you investigate slowness?
questions.answer: The browser resolves the host, establishes a connection, sends the request, receives HTML, parses it, discovers subresources, builds style and layout information, paints, and runs JavaScript that may attach behavior or hydrate UI. Measure before guessing: network timing, server response, render-blocking resources, long main-thread tasks, layout shifts, and hydration work point to different fixes.
questions.tip: Give a short pipeline first, then choose one measured bottleneck to discuss deeply.

questions.question: Why can an element with a very large z-index still appear behind another element?
questions.answer: z-index is compared inside stacking contexts. A child cannot escape its parent’s stacking context to outrank an element in a higher external context. Properties such as positioned z-index, transform, opacity below 1, and isolation can create stacking contexts. Inspect the context tree, not only the numeric value.
questions.tip: A larger number is not global across the whole page.

questions.question: What is the difference between layout, paint, and compositing work during an animation?
questions.answer: Layout calculates geometry, paint draws pixels, and compositing combines already painted layers. Animating width or top can require layout and paint, while transform and opacity can often be handled during compositing. That is a useful default, but measure because layer creation and memory also have costs.
questions.tip: Connect the answer to frame budget and DevTools performance measurements.
